Welcome to my portfolio

Caleb (Kwan Ho) Leung

Software engineer working across AI and data systems.

Building reliable systems to process, organize, and retrieve information for AI applications.

I am a software engineer interested in AI and working across the agent and data layers of production systems. My work focuses on backend engineering, distributed processing, and reliable data pipelines.

At IntellPro, my work includes designing scalable text-extraction and document-transformation services, developing a custom financial-document chunking algorithm and supporting library, and owning the distributed embedding stage—where I built its rate limiting, retries, worker orchestration, concurrency control, dead-letter queue handling, and state-machine-based job coordination. I have also applied agent workflows specifically to metadata extraction.

These contributions are part of a broader production document-processing pipeline that I work on alongside the team. The pipeline handles approximately 3,000 documents per day across more than 10 integrations.

As a first-generation college graduate, I earned a B.S. in Mathematics with a concentration in Financial Mathematics and a minor in Economics from Baruch College. I am currently pursuing an M.S. in Computer Science from Georgia Tech.

Personal projects

Projects & Research

In development

Anime MCP

I’m building a retrieval system for anime-character information, exposed through an MCP server. My current focus is indexing and retrieval, with ranking, hybrid fusion, and context expansion as areas of development and evaluation.

Research questions & reading

How should lexical and semantic scores be combined when their score distributions differ? I’m studying score normalization and hybrid fusion, with relevance calibration and query-adaptive weighting as follow-up questions.

  • An Analysis of Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval
  • Score distribution models: assumptions, intuition, and robustness to score manipulation
  • Classifier Calibration: A survey on how to assess and improve predicted class probabilities
  • Query Performance Prediction for Neural IR: Are We There Yet?

Training

I train for upper-body development and better jumping. My week includes five lifting sessions, Sunday jump practice, and a Wednesday rest day.

I’m temporarily adjusting my training around an elbow injury, so some movements are currently limited.

View my weekly routine
Monday · Short upper-body session
Machine shoulder press, machine chest press, chest-supported machine row, seated dumbbell lateral raise, reverse pec deck.
Tuesday · Lower-body maintenance
Front squat, Bulgarian split squat, back extension, single-leg press, single-leg seated hamstring curl, calf raise.
Wednesday · Rest
Rest day.
Thursday · Medium upper-body session
Machine chest and shoulder presses, Gironda-style and seated dumbbell lateral raises, single-arm incline machine press, pec deck, reverse pec deck.
Friday · Back
Chest-supported machine row, angled pulldown / high row, reverse pec deck.
Saturday · Longer upper-body session
Machine shoulder and chest presses, Gironda-style lateral raise, single-arm incline machine press, pec deck, reverse pec deck, machine ab crunch.
Sunday · Jump and dunk practice
One-foot jump progression.

留学生へのアドバイス

Advice for International Students

What I would prepare differently for studying and building a career in America. These are personal suggestions; your goals and budget may differ.

1. Choose a degree with a career plan

If your goal is working in the U.S., I would consider a STEM-eligible program that fits your interests and target jobs. Check the exact program’s STEM OPT eligibility with the school, and plan for OPT and possible employer-sponsored H-1B early. Eligible students can apply for a 24-month STEM OPT extension after the initial post-completion OPT period of up to 12 months, allowing up to 36 months in total if approved. Those two extra years can give a sponsoring employer more opportunities to register you for the annual H-1B selection process (lottery), depending on timing and continued eligibility; selection is not guaranteed. Neither a degree nor STEM OPT guarantees a job or long-term status.

2. Plan the full path for a theoretical degree

With a theoretical subject such as pure mathematics, I would plan beyond the degree title. Proof-based study can involve a long learning curve before you are ready for independent research, and an undergraduate degree alone may not prepare you for a specific job. Look at actual entry-level roles and the coding, statistics, applied knowledge, or experience they require. Do not assume the degree by itself will lead to U.S. employment or sponsorship.

Before committing, decide whether you want to work after your bachelor’s or pursue a master’s or PhD, and whether you are prepared for the academic demands and extra years. For an academic research career, plan for doctoral study. Work out the full cost: tuition, living expenses, funding conditions, and income you would forgo. Keep an alternative plan if funding, admission, or your interests change.

One route worth comparing is an affordable undergraduate degree outside the U.S., followed by a U.S. master’s. I would compare specific programs in Japan, Taiwan, the UK, or Australia, including the option of studying at home. None is automatically cheaper: compare total costs, scholarships, course length, language requirements, and whether the degree meets the U.S. graduate program’s admissions prerequisites.

3. Be clear about why you are going

A year of cultural exchange can be worthwhile on its own. If learning English is the main goal, I would compare options in the UK and Australia before paying for a U.S. program. Compare tuition, housing and course length rather than assume one country is always cheaper. If building an overseas career is the goal, research the programs, job market and work-authorization requirements before enrolling.

4. Start preparing before you arrive

I would build practical coding skills before university—perhaps through an affordable short coding bootcamp at home, even for physics, chemistry or math. Compare cost and quality; a certificate is not a degree or job guarantee. Open LinkedIn early, build projects, meet people and learn internship recruiting timelines instead of waiting until graduation.

Check current requirements: STEM OPT · H-1B
